title: Cu-doped zeolite imidazole framework (ZIF-8) for effective electrocatalytic CO2 reduction
abstract: Electrochemical CO2 reduction is a beneficial process for converting CO2 into useful hydrocarbons, chemicals, and fuels. Many catalysts have been tested before for CO2 electroreduction however achieving good stability, activity, and selectivity of the required product remains a challenge. In this work, we demonstrate the solvothermal synthesis and characterization of Cu-doped ZIF-8 catalysts with varying Cu+2 doping and applying them in the electrochemical CO2 reduction process. Cu30%ZIF-8 showed the highest current density of -40 mA cm 2 at -2.1 V vs. Ag/AgCl and better selectivity for CH4 and CO compared to previous works on Cu electrodes. This high activity of the Cu-doped ZIF-8 catalyst is because of the crystalline nanostructure of our catalyst with sufficient copper active metal sites and N-content, micro-meso dual-porosity nature of the structure, and broad surface area of zeolite imidazole framework to work on.

Cu-doped zeolite imidazole framework (ZIF-8) for effective electrocatalytic CO2 reduction
Awais Ahmad a, Naseem Iqbal a,*, Tayyaba Noor b, Ahmed Hassan a, Usman Ali Khan a, Abdul Wahab a, Muhammad Arslan Raza a, Sheeraz Ashraf a
a U.S-Pakistan Center for Advanced Studies in Energy (USPCAS-E), National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST) H-12, Islamabad, Pakistan b School of Chemical and Materials Engineering (SCME), National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST), H-12, Islamabad, Pakistan

Keywords: Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction Cu2+ doped ZIF-8 Faradaic efficiency Current density Surface area
A B S T R A C T
Electrochemical CO2 reduction is a beneficial process for converting CO2 into useful hydrocarbons, chemicals, and fuels. Many catalysts have been tested before for CO2 electroreduction however achieving good stability, activity, and selectivity of the required product remains a challenge. In this work, we demonstrate the solvothermal synthesis and characterization of Cu-doped ZIF-8 catalysts with varying Cu+2 doping and applying them in the electrochemical CO2 reduction process. Cu30%ZIF-8 showed the highest current density of -40 mA cm− 2 at -2.1 V vs. Ag/AgCl and better selectivity for CH4 and CO compared to previous works on Cu electrodes. This high activity of the Cu-doped ZIF-8 catalyst is because of the crystalline nanostructure of our catalyst with sufficient copper active metal sites and N-content, micro-meso dual-porosity nature of the structure, and broad surface area of zeolite imidazole framework to work on.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has increased from 280 to 400 ppm since the late 19th century [1]. Renewable energy resources are the alternative but the upcoming future still holds the main source of energy to be fossil fuel [2]. The current situation forces us to find solutions to prevent emissions and convert that CO2 into useful products to avoid extreme environmental issues [3]. The electroreduction [4–9] of carbon dioxide provides a viable route to a society free of carbon emissions while also providing renewable energy generation and storage [10–14]. The production of C1 feedstock and fuel by CO2 electrocatalytic reduction is of great promise as it would potentially close the carbon anthropogenic cycle [15].
A huge number of heterogeneous catalysts have been implemented for CO2 reduction. Among the transition metals especially copper-based materials are found to form methane, high carbon hydrocarbons, and alcohols because of their ability to reduce energy barrier [2,15–19]. For example, Cuprous oxide (Cu2O) has been studied for the reduction of CO2 to ethylene [20]. But the reduction of Cu+ to Cu◦ greatly reduces the stability of catalyst during the CO2 reduction. Also, the aggregation of pristine Cu2O affects the selectivity of the reduction process. In the latest work cubic Cu2O dispersed on nitrogen-doped carbon (NCS) showed excellent stability for CO2 reduction to ethylene at -1.3 V vs. (reversible
hydrogen electrode) with faradaic efficiency of 24.7 % [16]. This shows that improvement in selectivity and stability of the catalyst is crucial for an efficient reaction which leads to high current density and faradaic efficiency and, better performance. The high energy alcohols mainly methanol show a hurdle for their formation from CO2 conversion but their significance towards improving fuel economy and reducing emissions is cutting edge [19,21]. Copper selenide material has been reported to achieve relatively higher selectivity towards methanol [22].
One of the main strategies towards improving the performance of the catalyst is to mitigate its cons by forming a composite with another supporting material. Since 1900, a new generation of the catalyst has been studied which consist of metal ions and organic linkers to form up to three-dimensional network [23–25]. These crystalline porous materials are known as Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOFs) [26–44] have phenomenon physicochemical properties like high porosity, broad surface area, chemically tunable structures, and low density [45–47]. Zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIFs) [23,25,26,48–52], introduced by Yaghi et al. [53] as a subclass of MOFs, have been known to show remarkable chemical and thermal stability. These materials constitute the spatial arrangement of metal ions and imidazolate ligands and are formed in zeolite topologies similar to zeolites having a structure with cavities and nano-sized channels [53–55].
The most famous and in-work member of the ZIF family is ZIF-8

which has a sodalite (SOD) structure having a connection between zinc clusters and Hmim linker with 1.2 nm cages and small apertures of size 3.4 A◦ [54]. Due to their vastly suitable tailorable functionality and porosity ZIF-8 has been employed for catalysis, separation, CO2 capture and energy storage, and in various other applications [55–58]. ZIF-8 possesses excellent adsorption capabilities [59] and is reported for effective electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to carbon monoxide with 69.8 % faradaic efficiency [55]. But their selectivity and yield towards the formation of hydrocarbons like methane are very low.
In this work, we report the solvothermal preparation of Cu2+-doped ZIF-8 material. Varying copper doping in ZIF-8 was used to understand its effect on the catalyst for CO2 electrochemical reduction performance. The prepared catalysts structure, morphology, thermal stability, surface area, and porosity were characterized. After that, the catalysts were tested for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. The Cu2+ based ZIF-8 catalysts were found to be valuable in achieving promising activity for CO2 reduction process.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: Zinc nitrate hexahydrate (Zn(NO3)2.6H2O, >98 %, Aldrich), 2-methylimidazole (MeIm, purity 99 %, Merck), copper nitrate trihydrate (Cu (NO3)2.3H2O, Aldrich), methanol (>99.9 %, Aldrich), and DI water (18.2 MK cm). All materials were purchased and used as available.

sections.heading: 2.2.1. Synthesis of Cu-doped ZIF-8 catalyst
sections.text:
Cu-doped ZIF-8 samples were synthesized following a method pre-
viously reported with some modifications [25]. Cu(NO3)2.3H2O and Zn (NO3)2.6H2O precursors were mixed in 40 mL methanol to form a solution A. Cu(NO3)2 to Zn(NO3)2 molar percentage was 10 % (total 3.54 mmol). 2.301 g of 2-methylimidazole was added in 40 mL of methanol to form solution B. Then solution B was added to solution A with continuous stirring under the N2 atmosphere at room temperature and the reaction mixture was stirred for 90 min. The aging of the solution was
done for 24 h. Then the precipitate was separated by centrifugation (3500 rpm, 15 min) and washed with methanol 3 times. After that, the material was dried in air overnight and then in a vacuum oven at 70 ◦C for 24 h before further use. Samples were also prepared for the molar percentage of Cu(NO3)2 to Zn(NO3)2 of 20 % and 30 % using the same procedure.

sections.heading: 2.3. Material characterization
sections.text: Powder X-ray diffraction of the samples was done by using D8 ADVANCE, CuKR, λ =1.54 Å (BRUKER, Germany). The XRD measurements were taken for 2θ values from 5 to 90 degrees. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) were performed using a VEGA3/TESCAN, 51–ADD0007 (Brno, Czech Republic) to understand the structural morphology and elemental composition of the sample. The samples were coated with gold and the electron beam was set at 20 eV. To analyze the thermal stability of the catalyst material thermogravimetric measurements were performed on a DTG-60H Thermo Gravimetric Analyzer (Shimadzu Japan). The material was placed in platinum crucibles and the sample was heated from room temperature to 900 ⁰C under air with a ramp of 10 ⁰C min− 1. To identify the functional groups in the sample FTIR Agilent cary 630 (Agilent USA) was used. Transmittance spectra were taken from 650− 1400 cm− 1. Using BET Nova 2200e (Quantachrome, USA) having liquid nitrogen (− 196 ◦C) the N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms of the sample were taken. Before the analysis sample was degassed at 80 ⁰C. Using isotherms BET surface area, micropore volume, and micropore size of each sample were calculated.

sections.heading: 2.4.1. Working electrode preparation
sections.text:
The glassy carbon working electrode was first sonicated in an
acetone/water bath and then dipped in ethanol and water for washing. The washed electrode was polished with 1 mm alumina powder by scrubbing the electrode surface in the slurry of powder for 2 min. The polished electrode is then coated with catalyst ink. 25 mg catalyst material was dispersed in 1 mL ethanol and 40 μL Nafion and then sonicated

for 2 h to form a homogenous dispersion. About 11.5 μL dispersion was then drop-casted on the working electrode and allowed to dry at room temperature. Catalyst loading was calculated to be approximately 4.06 mg cm− 2. The well-prepared electrode was then used for electrochemical testing.

sections.heading: 2.4.2. Electrochemical CO2 reduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical H-cell was used for performing all the reactions. The
cell used was of two compartments separated by a glass fritz. The
working electrode and the reference electrode (Ag/AgCl) were kept in the cathodic compartment. The counter electrode was Pt and was kept in an anodic compartment. 35 mL of 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous electrolyte was used in each compartment. After setting up the cell for testing initially N2 was purged through the electrolyte for 30 min to make an inert atmosphere followed by CO2 purge through the electrolyte in the cathode compartment for 30 min until the electrolyte gets saturated to a pH of 6.8. During this, the CO2 gas flow rate was kept at 30 mL min− 1. After that linear sweep voltammetry measurements were taken by applying potential through an electrochemical workstation.

sections.heading: 2.4.3. Constant potential electrolysis
sections.text: A bulk electrolysis experiment was performed by keeping the gas flow rate at 10 mL min− 1 and applying a constant potential across the working electrode in the range from -1.2 V to -1.6 V vs. Ag/AgCl (reference electrode). Each constant potential experiment was performed for 20 min and the gas sample was collected at the end of each process through a syringe and analyzed by a gas chromatography-TCD to detect the gas products formed. After each reaction, the cell was cleaned with DI water and ethanol and the fritz was dipped in 0.1 M H2SO4 to regenerate it.

sections.heading: 3.1. Synthesis and characterization of catalyst
sections.text:
The copper doped ZIF-8 catalyst was prepared by mixing solutions of Zn(NO3)2, Cu(NO3)2, and 2-methylimidazole in the N2 atmosphere for 90 min (Fig. 1). Afterward, the aging process was done which allows crystals to grow into proper shape. Centrifugation, washing, and drying of these samples were done before characterization. Molar percentages of 10 %, 20 %, and 30 % of Cu(NO3)2 to Zn(NO3)2 were used to prepare

three different samples named Cu10%ZIF-8, Cu20%ZIF-8, and Cu30% ZIF-8 respectively. As reported in previous work, further increasing the copper doping will cause the ZIF-8 structure to collapse [25]. It was observed that with increasing the copper doping the color of the samples changes from white to light brown color as shown in Fig. 2.
The structure and morphology of ZIF-8 and Cu-ZIF-8 samples were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy. The images (Fig. 3) show rhombic dodecahedral cubic structure for all samples which is characteristic of ZIF-8 structure [60]. This shows that Cu-doping does not alter the crystal morphology of the Zn-imidazole framework. As the copper content increases from 20 % to 30 %, the average diameter of Cu-ZIF-8 nanocrystals enlarges. This is because the generation of new nuclei decreases and already formed nuclei grow through further addition of 2-methylimidazole (Melm) and solvated Cu+2 and Zn+2 species as confirmed by literature [25]. The elemental analysis of the samples was
done by EDS which gives Cu content of 0.26 %, 0.53 %, and 1.02 % for Cu10%ZIF-8, Cu20%ZIF-8, and Cu30%ZIF-8 respectively given in Table 1.
The powder X-ray diffraction of the samples was shown in Fig. 4. ZIF8 and Cu-doped ZIF-8 sample patterns are similar showing addition of Cu does not affect the crystal structure of ZIF-8 which is confirmed from the literature [61]. The main reason for this is that the ionic size of both Cu2+ (0.71 Å) and Zn2+ (0.74 Å) ions are close which maintains the structural integrity of the ZIF-8 framework. The similarity in pattern and morphology shows that Cu-ZIF-8 has body-centered cubic crystal lattice symmetry as in ZIF-8 [25]. It was observed that with the increase of Cu doping in the ZIF-8 structure, the crystallite size was found to increase from 31.7 nm to 41.62 nm calculated from XRD. Fig. 5 shows the thermogravimetric analysis of all Cu-based ZIF-8 samples. The Cu10%ZIF-8 sample shows thermal stability up to 430 ◦C. The small weight loss of 10 % before that was moisture and volatile residual 2-methylimidazole (MeIm) molecules. After that the decomposition of the organic linker and Zn metal takes place and the weight sharply reduces until 542 ◦C. From 430 ◦C to 542 ◦C the sharp weight loss of 60–65 % was observed for Cu10%ZIF-8 which is consistent with previous work [25]. It was observed that higher Cu percentage catalysts

of Cu20%ZIF-8 and Cu30%ZIF-8 have more thermal stability which can be mainly attributed to the strength of the coordination bond or covalent bond in the framework. So as Cu doping increases, the Zn ions reduce and thus increase the overall stability of the catalyst which is consistent with literature work [62]. The final residue for the Cu10%ZIF-8, Cu20% ZIF-8, and Cu30%ZIF-8 catalyst was 35 %, 24 % and 16 % respectively.
FTIR analysis of the catalyst materials is shown in Fig. 6. ZIF-8, Cu10%ZIF-8, Cu20%ZIF-8 and Cu30%ZIF-8 all have the similar peaks and consistent with literature [63,64]. 2-methylimidazole (MeIm) peak appeared at 694 cm− 1 (C–H bend). The peak at 1147 cm− 1 confirms (=C–H) in-plane deformation vibration. (=C–H) in-plane bending occurs at 995 cm− 1, while the CH2 wagging transmits light at 1313 cm− 1. The asymmetric bend of CH3 and CH2 gives response at 1384 cm− 1 and 1427 cm− 1 respectively. Carbon-carbon double bond stretch (C–C stretch) is assigned peak at 1456 cm− 1 while (C–N stretch) has peaked at 1585 cm− 1 The two narrow small peaks at 2931 cm− 1 and 3137 cm− 1 confirm (C–H) symmetric stretch and (=C–H) stretch respectively. To analyze the absorption properties of ZIF-8 and Cu-doped ZIF-8
samples, N2 adsorption-desorption analysis was done. The generated isotherms (Fig. 7) were of type I which indicated that our samples have microporous structures. It was observed that for all samples, the volume of gas adsorbed increases two times, first at low relative pressure (P/Po) >0.08 and then at a high P/Po value near 1 which confirms the dual micro and mesoporous nature of Cu doped ZIF-8 samples [25]. The BET surface area was calculated to be 1620 m2 g− 1, 1967 m2 g− 1,1772 m2 g− 1, and 1238 m2 g− 1 for ZIF-8, Cu10%ZIF-8, Cu20%ZIF-8 and Cu30% ZIF-8 respectively as shown in Table 2. The BJH pore size distribution
for Cu-ZIF-8 samples is in the range of 1.8–2.32 nm similar to ZIF-8 (Fig. 7).

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical performance
sections.text:
The catalytic activity for CO2 reduction of Cu-doped ZIF-8 samples was tested on a glassy carbon working electrode in 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. Linear sweep voltammetry was done in the potential range of -0.8 V to -2.1 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) to check the response of current density against the applied potential for Cu30%ZIF-8, Cu20%ZIF-8, and Cu10%ZIF-8 as shown in Fig. 8. Among them, Cu30%ZIF-8 showed the highest current density of -40 mA cm− 2 at -2.1 V which is identical to the previously reported work [22]. Fig. 8(a–c) compares LSV traces for different Cu-doped samples in N2 and CO2 purged electrolytes. For Cu30%ZIF-8 the current starts to increase early at -1 V in CO2 with a positive shifted onset potential of 400 mV compared to N2 which shows that CO2 is reducing as confirmed by literature [55]. Although Cu30% ZIF-8 shows
lower current activity in N2 compared to CO2 but it is still more than Cu20%ZIF-8 and Cu10%ZIF-8 catalytic response in CO2. The high current shown by the Cu30%ZIF-8 for CO2 reduction is attributed to the availability of more active copper metal sites which increases the overall performance than other catalysts. At -2.1 V, Cu20% ZIF-8 gives a slightly higher peak current density of 18.5 mA cm− 2 then Cu10%ZIF-8 value of 18.3 mA cm− 2 (Fig. 8d). The main reason for this is more copper nodes present for CO2 reduction in Cu20%ZIF-8 having a low surface area compared to Cu10%ZIF-8. The fact that Cu30%ZIF-8 current density is

Journal of CO2 Utilization 48 (2021) 101523
almost more than double of Cu20%ZIF-8 can not only be attributed to the more copper sites but also the high N-content (Table 1) in Cu30% ZIF-8 compared to Cu20%ZIF-8. In previous work, it was reported that more N-content in the carbon structure improves the activity for CO2 electroreduction by promoting proton-electron transfer [3]. The high nitrogen content present in the structure helps in the proper dispersion of Cu nanocrystals throughout the catalyst [16]. Although Cu10%ZIF-8 has the highest N-content among all catalysts and better surface area but doesn’t have enough copper sites to function with as compared to other catalysts and consequently has the lowest current density. The high
copper content remains the key factor that greatly improves the performance of our catalyst. As shown in SEM images (Fig. 3), the Cu30% ZIF-8 crystals are more properly shaped and not clustered compared to Cu10%ZIF-8 and Cu20%ZIF-8 which helps in catalysis reaction by allowing the CO2 molecules to properly adsorb on more active metal sites. The N-content in the structure of Cu30%ZIF-8 allows active copper nodes to properly distribute in the structure on large crystals of catalyst. This increases the current density and electroreduction performance.
Constant potential electrolysis or bulk electrolysis was performed within the narrow potential range of -1.2 V to -1.6 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) to
A. Ahmad et al.
Journal of CO2 Utilization 48 (2021) 101523
evaluate the different products of CO2 reduction and their faradaic efficiency. Using the gas chromatography technique CO, H2 and methane were the only detected gaseous products. As shown in Fig. 9d), the hydrogen evolution reaction dominates until at -1.2 V vs. Ag/AgCl and is the peak point for H2 formation with Cu20%ZIF-8 catalyst giving the least H2 faradaic efficiency of 80% among all the Cu doped ZIF-8 catalysts tested at this potential. The hydrogen evolution reaction suppresses and its faradaic efficiency starts to decrease above -1.2 V vs. Ag/AgCl which gives way for CO2 reduction process. Carbon monoxide is the first CO2 reduction C1 product and as potential becomes more negative its faradaic efficiency increases until − 1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl where it reaches its maximum value. From Fig. 9c), Cu10%ZIF-8 shows the highest CO formation performance of 62.26 % at -1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl and requiring less over-potential as compared to previous work [55]. This high selectivity and lower over-potential for CO on Cu10%ZIF-8 is regarded to the availability of a very high surface area of 1927 m2 g− 1 and high adsorption capacity for CO2 molecules on Cu2+ and Zn2+ active sites and coordinated unsaturated atoms [65]. Also, more Zn nodes availability in Cu10%ZIF-8 improves the selectivity for CO formation [55]. The highest N-content of Cu10%ZIF-8 also helps in the electron transfer which lowers the energy barrier for COOH* formation which is the intermediate for CO production [3]. Similarly, Cu20%ZIF-8 and Cu30%ZIF-8 show a maximum CO faradaic efficiency of 46.88 % and 48.2 % respectively as shown in Fig. 9c).
Methane is an important CO2 reduction product. Its production is low at less negative potential but gradually increases as potential reaches − 1.4 V vs. Ag/AgCl (Fig. 9b). Above -1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl CO starts decreasing because the more negative potential increases the pH of the solution and reduces CO2 molecules present which allows the conversion of CO to hydrocarbons like methane as confirmed by literature [66]. Cu30%ZIF-8 achieves the highest catalytic activity for methane production with a faradaic efficiency of 35.21 % at -1.6 V vs. Ag/AgCl having a high partial current density of 2.86 mA cm− 2 Fig. 9e). This selectively and partial current density is
achieved at less negative potential compared to previous works on methane formation by Cu single crystals surfaces Cu(111) [67] and polycrystalline copper [68]. The results in Fig. 9b) indicate that as copper content increases and Zn ions drop in the zeolite imidazole framework, the methane generation capability of the catalyst increases overcoming the energy barrier for hydrocarbons generation. This is because of the copper ion’s special ability to form hydrocarbons.
Fig. 9f compares current stability graph during bulk electrolysis for the catalyst Cu30%ZIF-8 at -1.5 V, -1.4 V and -1.3 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) constant applied potentials for 20 min. The current density increases
gradually after dropping in the first 100 s initially while it stabilizes quickly at -1.5 V and then increases variably. This is because of the gas bubbling process occurring on the electrode surface as CO also starts adsorbing on the catalyst which varies the current passing through with time. The line is relatively more stable at -1.2 V vs. Ag/AgCl potential due to low bubbling and a gradual increase in current is taking place. The SEM analysis of the best performance catalyst Cu30%ZIF-8 after the stability test is shown in Fig. 10. It shows some large size crystals compared to an unused catalyst which is formed due to the reduction of copper sites. Other than that the small crystals are somewhere clustered together due to the Nafion binder used in ink formation for catalysis. At some sites, rhombic dodecahedral cubic morphology is maintained by the catalyst. The electrolyte, binder, and catalytic CO2 reduction have affected the shape pattern and morphology of the crystals.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, different Cu-doped ZIF-8 samples were synthesized with varying copper percentages for CO2 electro-reduction process. The Cu-doped ZIF-8 catalysts showed good selectivity for methane and CO while Cu30%ZIF-8 gives the highest CH4 faradaic efficiency of 35.21 % at -1.6 V vs. Ag/AgCl better compared to previous work on Cu electrode. Remarkably, Cu30%ZIF-8 also showed the highest current density of -40 mA cm− 2 at -2.1 V vs. Ag/AgCl comparable to the best activities. It was observed that with increasing the copper molar percentage the selectivity for methane increases. The morphology, surface area, high Ncontent, and proper accessibility of active metal catalytic sites play a key role in achieving high catalytic efficiency for the CO2 reduction reaction.
